claim: When engineers no longer read all generated code, execution evidence is needed to understand what the code actually did.
The episode frames observability as the way to compare expected behavior with what happened after execution.
Wide events preserve enough dimensions to investigate unknown failures later, instead of emitting only a few predefined metrics.
Observability is most useful in hindsight for questions that were not known when the system was built.
A trace and flame graph can reveal call order, repetition, timing, and unexpected branches without first reading every function.
Production traces may be sampled to learn system shape rather than kept for every request, which limits individual replay coverage.
Agents can inspect traces for reported failures because humans cannot review every trace manually.
Missing instrumentation removes the evidence needed for later debugging; generated code will not reliably add every required trace point on its own.
High-volume tracing creates storage and transport costs, so the system must choose an event model and collection boundary deliberately.
